The timeframe was sufficient to reasonably expect an association between the exposure and the outcome, if such an association existed. 3. The exposure measures (independent variables) were clearly defined, valid, reliable, and implemented consistently across all study participants. 4. The exposures were assessed more than once over time. 5. The outcome measures (dependent variables) were clearly defined, valid, reliable, and implemented consistently across all study participants. 6. The outcome assessors were blinded to the exposure status of the participants. 7. The loss to follow-up after baseline was 20% or less. 8. Key potential confounding variables were measured and statistically adjusted for their impact on the relationship between exposures and outcomes. Summary of PICO Question 2a: A single, uniform treatment regimen for all leprosy cases was evaluated for its effectiveness and safety compared to the two currently recommended regimens: one for multibacillary (MB) leprosy involving a combination of three drugs for 12 months, and one for paucibacillary (PB) leprosy involving a combination of two drugs for six months. Study by Rao PN (2009): Design and Setting: Moderate-quality, open comparative study conducted in India with 64 participants. Outcome Measures: Clinical assessment, histopathological assessment, reactions, adverse effects, and therapy tolerance. Results for PB Patients: Intervention groups: Uniform MDT (U-MDT) and Regular MDT (R-MDT). At 6 months: Histopathological improvement was observed in 91% (10/11) of U-MDT patients and 80% (4/5) of R-MDT patients. At 12 months: Improvement was 100% (9/9) for U-MDT and 86% (6/7) for R-MDT. At 18 months: Improvement was 83% (5/6) for U-MDT and 100% (1/1) for R-MDT. At 24 months: Improvement was 100% (1/1) for U-MDT and 67% (2/3) for R-MDT. Results for MB Patients: At 12 months: Histopathological improvement was 100% (4/4) for U-MDT and 77% (7/9) for R-MDT. At 18 months: Improvement was 50% (1/2) for U-MDT and 100% (12/12) for R-MDT. At 24 months: Improvement was 100% (6/6) for R-MDT. Adverse Effects: In PB patients, two developed dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome, and one developed acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) within the first four weeks of therapy. Clofazimine pigmentation was observed in 11 patients (2 PB and 9 MB). Therapy Tolerance: Tolerance to therapy was generally good. Study by Manickam (2016): Design and Setting: Moderate-quality, single-arm open field trial conducted in India and China with 3389 participants. Outcome Measures: New lesions, relapse, reactions, disability, neuritis, and other events. Results: No significant differences in outcomes for PB patients treated with U-MDT compared to R-MDT. PICO Question 2b: Which treatment regimen demonstrates better effectiveness and safety for leprosy patients with rifampicin resistance, with or without associated resistance to dapsone or ofloxacin? Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted using MEDLINE and Embase for studies published between 1996 and January 2017. The search included MeSH terms and text words for leprosy, drug resistance, and rifampicin resistance, combined using Boolean operators. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled clinical trials assessing antibiotic treatments for PB and MB leprosy with rifampicin resistance were included. Results: No studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. PICO Question 3a: Is there an effective and safe chemoprophylaxis regimen for preventing leprosy among contacts of leprosy patients and other high-risk populations under programmatic conditions? Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted using MEDLINE and Embase for studies published between 2010 and January 2017. The search included MeSH terms and text words for leprosy, chemoprophylaxis, and post-exposure prophylaxis, combined using Boolean operators. Randomized controlled trials and cohort studies with control groups assessing chemoprophylaxis for leprosy prevention were included. Results: One large RCT (COLEP) and a follow-up study were included. Single-dose rifampicin (SDR) significantly reduced the proportion of contacts diagnosed with leprosy at 1-2 years post-intervention. SDR was found to be cost-effective, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of $158 per additional case prevented. A qualitative study reported that most participants were willing to take prophylaxis if their contact was diagnosed with leprosy, despite concerns about privacy and stigma. Conclusion: Uniform MDT regimens showed promising results for both PB and MB leprosy patients, but further studies with larger sample sizes are needed. SDR chemoprophylaxis is effective and cost-efficient for preventing leprosy among contacts, with high acceptability among participants.
